topics.title: FILES OF PAGES OF RECORDS / HEAP FILE

questions.prompt: Which containment hierarchy is correct in this storage model?
options: A page must contain a database
Each field contains a file
A logical file contains pages, and each page contains records
A record contains logical files, and each file contains pages
questions.explanation: The containment hierarchy is file → page → record. A field is a smaller component within a record.

questions.prompt: Must a logical database file correspond to exactly one operating-system file?
options: Yes, this is always part of its definition
Only when it contains more than one record
Only when it stores text
No, it can span multiple operating-system files or machines
questions.explanation: A logical abstraction does not require a one-to-one correspondence with physical files.

questions.prompt: Which operation can the file layer's API support?
options: Fetch a record by its RID
Track reference bits to select a CLOCK victim
Choose between a hash join and a merge join
Move the disk head to the track containing a block
questions.explanation: The record/file layer understands record identifiers and scans. Hardware details and query-plan choices belong to other layers.

questions.prompt: What ordering does a heap file impose on its records?
options: Always descending order of salary
No required ordering by a search key
Always sorted by the primary key
The ordering of a binary heap is mandatory
questions.explanation: A heap file is not the heap data structure used for a priority queue. It simply has no required sort order.

questions.prompt: As a heap file grows or shrinks, what must the system track?
options: Only column names and types in the schema
Only the root page of an arbitrary index
The file's pages, their free space, and the records on each page
Only tuples returned by SELECT
questions.explanation: These three kinds of metadata support record and file management. Query text cannot replace them.

topics.title: HEAP FILE: LINKED LIST / PAGE DIRECTORY

questions.prompt: How does the linked-list heap organisation in the slides separate pages?
options: Pages with primary keys from pages with foreign keys
Pages with fixed-length keys from pages with variable-length keys
Pages that were recently read from pages that have never been read
Full pages from pages with free space
questions.explanation: The lists distinguish pages that may have room for insertion. Their membership does not depend on the values stored in the records.

questions.prompt: Why might finding a page for a large record through a free-space list require many reads?
options: Many pages have free space, but not enough for that record
Every page is completely empty
No page has a header
A linked list automatically deletes large records
questions.explanation: Having some free space does not mean having enough bytes. The system may need to inspect many candidate pages.

questions.prompt: What essential information does a page-directory entry store?
options: Only the relation's schema, with no page metadata
A data-page ID and the number of free bytes
All record contents from the data page
Only next/previous pointers, with no free-space information
questions.explanation: The directory summarises each page's identity and available space so the system can choose an insertion location.

questions.prompt: Why can a page directory reduce the I/O needed to find space for an insertion?
options: The directory automatically increases the physical page capacity
Every record is stored directly in the directory
One directory page describes many data pages
An insertion never needs to read or write a data page
questions.explanation: Reading a few metadata pages can reveal many candidates. The selected data page may still need to be read and written.

questions.prompt: A directory reports free space of P1=20, P2=90, and P3=40 bytes. A record needs 60 bytes, with no additional overhead. Which page has enough space?
options: P1
P3
All three pages
P2
questions.explanation: Only P2 has at least 60 bytes, because 90≥60. The other pages have some free space, but not enough.

questions.prompt: A page has a 16-byte header and 24-byte records, numbered from 1. At what byte offset does record 4 begin?
questions.explanation: The offset is 16+(4−1)×24=88. The first record starts immediately after the header, so the record number is reduced by one.

questions.prompt: Where is a new record normally inserted in a packed page that still has space?
options: Always in a different file
After the last existing record
Always before the header
Always in a hole in the middle, even though a packed layout has no holes
questions.explanation: A packed layout keeps records in a contiguous region. A new record is appended to the end of the occupied region.

questions.prompt: What risk arises when a middle record is deleted and the last record is moved into its place?
options: The moved record must change its schema
The page automatically becomes an index page
The moved record's position-based RID changes
Its RID cannot change because every layout uses slot indirection
questions.explanation: Moving a record changes an identifier based directly on its position. It does not automatically change the record's byte length.

questions.prompt: If every field has a fixed size, what can be inferred?
options: Each record must occupy an entire page
All fields must have the same length as one another
Records must be sorted by their first field
Record size is fixed if the metadata layout is also fixed
questions.explanation: A fixed sum of field lengths, together with fixed metadata, gives a fixed record length. It does not require one page per record.

questions.prompt: A page has 512 bytes, a 32-byte header, and 30-byte fixed-length records, with no other overhead. How many records fit?
questions.explanation: There are floor((512−32)/30)=16 record slots. Rounding up would exceed the page's capacity.

questions.prompt: What does the bitmap of an unpacked page primarily record?
options: The sorted key values on the page
Which slots are occupied and which are empty
Whether each field in a record is NULL
The reference bit of each buffer frame
questions.explanation: This bitmap tracks slot occupancy. It does not store query results or field-level NULL information.

questions.prompt: What is the main metadata change when deleting a record in a bitmap-based layout?
options: Delete every subsequent slot
Change every RID on the page
Mark the slot as empty
Always move the last record into that slot
questions.explanation: The layout permits gaps, so other records do not have to move. Their positions can remain unchanged.

questions.prompt: Which slots does the free list link together?
options: Occupied slots containing records with the same key
Buffer frames with pinCount=0
NULL fields within a record
Empty slots
questions.explanation: The list helps locate unused slots. A NULL field within an existing record does not make that record's slot empty.

questions.prompt: When inserting a record into the slot at the head of a free list, what must change?
options: Use the head slot, then move the head to the next free slot
Keep the head pointing to the occupied slot so it can be reused immediately
Copy the new record into every free slot
Delete all records after the selected slot
questions.explanation: The occupied slot is no longer free. The head must point to the next remaining free slot.

questions.prompt: The free list is 2→5→8. A record in slot 4 is deleted, and that slot is added at the front. What is the new list?
questions.explanation: Adding the newly freed slot at the front makes slot 4 point to the previous head, slot 2.

questions.prompt: How is a RID represented in a slotted page?
options: A table name and a tuple's position in a query result
A field ID and an offset within a record
A page ID and a slot ID
A page ID and the record's direct physical byte offset
questions.explanation: The slot directory provides an indirection from the RID to the record's byte offset. The RID does not contain that offset directly.

questions.prompt: A record moves from offset 700 to 800 within the same page, keeping its slot ID. What must be updated?
options: The external RID must change to the new offset even though the slot is unchanged
The field schema must change because the record moved
The page ID must change even though the record remains on the same page
The offset stored in the slot directory
questions.explanation: The external reference is (page ID,slot ID), so neither component changes. After moving the bytes from 700 to 800, set that same slot entry to offset 800. The next fetch follows the slot to the new position. Updating the index to store a raw offset would bypass this indirection.

questions.prompt: Why should deleting a record not arbitrarily renumber all the remaining slots?
options: External RIDs may refer to those slot IDs
Record bytes must never be moved
A slot directory must always be packed with no empty slots
Every slot ID is a business-level primary key
questions.explanation: Changing a slot's identity can invalidate external references. The record bytes can still be moved during compaction.

questions.prompt: A page has 1000 bytes and a 20-byte header. Each record needs 45 bytes plus a 4-byte slot entry. With no other overhead, how many records fit?
questions.explanation: Each record and its slot entry need 49 bytes. The available 980 bytes hold floor(980/49)=20 records.

questions.prompt: A page has enough total free space, but no sufficiently large contiguous region. What is an appropriate action within the page?
options: Keep the old offsets after moving the bytes
Assume enough total free bytes removes the need for a contiguous region
Compact or defragment the page, then update the offsets
Increase the length field without allocating actual bytes
questions.explanation: Compaction combines the gaps into a larger free region. Updating the directory preserves record identifiers while the bytes move.

questions.prompt: Must complete field-type information be repeated in every record?
options: Yes, each record must store the complete DDL text
Yes, the system catalog stores only query results
No schema information is needed at any layer
No, the schema can be stored in the system catalog
questions.explanation: The catalog stores a shared schema, avoiding repetition of the complete metadata in every record.

questions.prompt: Three fields have lengths of 4, 2, and 8 bytes, with no header. At what offset does the third field begin?
questions.explanation: The offset is the sum of the preceding field lengths: 4+2=6. It is not the length of the third field itself.

questions.prompt: What complication arises when a variable-length field's value contains its delimiter?
options: Every field must be padded to the same length
Escaping or another way to distinguish data from delimiters is needed
No field can be accessed even with a parser
The data type alone identifies every boundary, so escaping is unnecessary
questions.explanation: Without escaping or an equivalent convention, the parser cannot reliably distinguish field boundaries from delimiter characters inside a value.

questions.prompt: Why may length=0 be insufficient to distinguish NULL from an empty string?
options: NULL is always encoded as the character 0
A positive offset automatically proves that a field is not NULL
Both can have no payload bytes while having different meanings
An empty string and NULL always have identical semantics
questions.explanation: An empty string has a present value containing zero bytes. NULL marks a missing/unknown value and can also have no payload. A separate NULL bit distinguishes the two. Neither state means that the whole record has been deleted; slot occupancy is separate metadata.

questions.prompt: A record has a 12-byte fixed region followed by a 5-byte ASCII name. What are the name's offset and length?
questions.explanation: The offset identifies the start of the payload, and the length counts its bytes. The length is not the payload's ending position.
